english: She is learning to play the piano.
tip: 'çalmayı' = 'çal' + -ma + -yı: -ma turns a verb into a noun 'playing', then object-marker -yı marks it as the thing being learned.

english: She spread honey on her bread for breakfast.
tip: 'ekmeğine': the final k of 'ekmek' softens to ğ before a vowel ending, so 'ekmek' plus its suffixes becomes 'ekmeğine'.

english: My grandmother made the stuffed grape leaves in the kitchen.
tip: 'dolmayı' is the object and 'yaptı' is the verb at the end: Turkish normally puts the verb last, so objects like 'dolmayı' come before it.

english: My name is Ali, nice to meet you.
tip: 'benim' in 'benim adım' is optional because 'adım' already means 'my name'. Add 'benim' only to stress whose name it is.

target: Bugünkü toplantı uzun ve yorucu oldu.
english: Today's meeting was long and tiring.
tip: 'bugünkü' = 'bugün' (today) + -kü: the -ki/-kü ending makes 'the one of that time', so 'bugünkü toplantı' = today's meeting.

target: Temiz hava için kalabalık şehirlerden uzaklaşmalıyız.
english: We should get away from crowded cities for clean air.
tip: 'uzaklaşmalıyız' = 'uzaklaş' + -malı + -yız: -malı/-meli means 'must' and -yız marks we, so 'we must move away'.

target: Memnun oldum, uzun süredir görüşmek istiyordum.
english: I'm glad to see you. I've been wanting to meet up for a long time.
tip: 'süredir' = 'süre' (time) + -dir: here -dir means 'for/since', so 'uzun süredir' means 'for a long time now'.

target: Sizin eviniz çok güzel, bahçesi de geniş.
english: Your house is very nice, its garden is also spacious.
tip: 'bahçesi' = 'bahçe' + -si: after a vowel-ending noun, a buffer s carries the -si ending, giving 'its garden'.

target: Dün gece hiç uyuyamadım, gürültü çok fazlaydı.
english: I couldn't sleep at all last night, the noise was too much.
tip: 'uyuyamadım' = I couldn't sleep: the -yama inside the verb means inability, so it's not 'didn't' but 'couldn't'.

target: Eski eşyaları atmak yerine ihtiyacı olanlara verelim.
english: Instead of throwing away old things let's give them to those in need.
tip: 'verelim' = let's give: adding -elim/-alım to a verb stem makes a 'let's do it' suggestion, like 'gidelim' = let's go.

target: Toplantı iki saat sürdü ve önemli kararlar aldık.
english: The meeting lasted two hours and we made important decisions.
tip: Turkish 'makes decisions' with 'almak' (to take): 'kararlar aldık' means we took, that is made, decisions.

target: Taze ekmek fırından yeni çıkmış, mis gibi kokuyor.
english: The fresh bread just came out of the oven, smells wonderful.
tip: 'çıkmış' uses -mış for something inferred rather than watched happen, fitting 'the bread has evidently just come out'.

target: Çok soğuk olmasına rağmen yine de yürüyüşe çıktık.
english: Although it was very cold, we still went for a walk.
tip: 'rağmen' (despite) makes the word before it take the -a ending: 'olmasına rağmen' = despite it being cold.

target: Pideci ustası hamuru çok ince açar.
english: The pide master rolls the dough very thin.
tip: 'pideci' = 'pide' + -ci: the -ci ending names the person who makes or sells something, so 'pideci' is the pide maker.

english: Have a safe journey!
tip: Turkish good-wishes often take the plural. 'yolculuklar' is the plural of 'yolculuk' (journey); 'iyi yolculuklar' means have a good trip.

english: They arrive nicely.
tip: The suffix -ce turns an adjective into a manner adverb. 'güzel' means nice, 'güzelce' means nicely.

english: They arrive excitedly.
tip: The suffix -la/-le means with and builds manner adverbs. 'heyecan' is excitement, 'heyecanla' means excitedly.

english: The post office is across from the park.
tip: A position word like 'karşısında' (across from) needs the owner marked with -ın: 'parkın karşısında' means across from the park.

english: Goodbye, have a good journey.
tip: 'güle güle' is said by the person staying to the one leaving. The one departing says 'hoşça kal' or 'hoşça kalın' instead.

english: Get well soon, we miss you.
tip: 'geçmiş olsun' is a fixed get-well phrase, literally may it be past; you say it to anyone sick or in trouble.

english: I was very pleased, sir.
tip: For pleased to meet you Turkish uses the past tense: 'memnun oldum' is literally I became pleased.

english: Take the second street on the left.
tip: A final k softens to ğ before a vowel ending. 'sokak' plus the -a ending becomes 'sokağa', meaning to the street.

english: Sorry, I disturbed you.
tip: 'kusura bakmayın' is a set apology, literally don't look at the fault, meaning no offense or excuse me.

english: Welcome back, we were waiting for you.
tip: Past continuous stacks -yor plus -du. 'bekliyor' (is waiting) becomes 'bekliyorduk', we were waiting.

english: I still can't decide; I need to think about it.
tip: To say need to, use the verb as a noun with a personal ending plus 'lazım'. 'düşünmem lazım' means I need to think.

english: My grandfather taught me how to play chess.
tip: A verb becomes an object with -ma plus the object marker -yı. 'oynamayı öğretti' means taught the playing, that is, taught how to play.

target: Henüz hazır değilim, beş dakika bekle.
english: I'm not ready yet, wait five minutes.
tip: Adjectives and nouns are negated with the separate word 'değil', not a suffix. 'hazır değilim' means I'm not ready.

english: The nurse took my blood pressure.
tip: The -u/-ı object ending marks a definite object. 'tansiyonumu' (my blood pressure) ends in -u because it's the specific thing measured.

english: We met with our friends and ate.
tip: The -ip ending chains verbs that share one final tense. 'buluşup yedik' means met up and ate; only 'yedik' carries the past.

english: The writer will write a book tomorrow.
tip: Future tense is -acak/-ecek. 'yaz' (write) plus -acak gives 'yazacak', will write.
